newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Further setback for Menem in Argentine labor court.
newsitem.headline: Further setback for Menem in Argentine labor court.

text.p: An Argentine labor court on Friday partially upheld two judges' rulings that President Carlos Menem's attempt to reform the country's labor laws by presidential decree is unconstitutional.

Three labor court judges threw out the government appeals on two of the three decrees which Menem signed in December -- and which sparked a December 26 general strike led by the main CGT labor federation.

They supported two colleagues' earlier rulings, contested by Menem, that two decrees letting the Labor Ministry revoke the validity of collective labor agreements and letting smaller companies sidestep unions in collective pay bargaining, violate Argentina's constitution.

But the judges ruled that the third decree authorizing the Labor Ministry to set the level of talks -- company-by-company or industry-wide -- if unions and employers cannot agree on this point, should be allowed.

One of the three labor judges sitting on the appeal, Juan Carlos Morando, told reporters the CGT's attempts to fight the decrees in court were legitimate because the decrees affected "not only the workers involved in the collective labor talks, but also the unions and the employers..."
He said article 14 of the Argentine constitution upheld the right of trade unions to participate in collective wage negotiations, just as it upheld the right to strike.
President Menem argues that these and further planned reforms of Argentina's outdated labor legislation are needed to bring down unemployment from its current 17.3 percent.
But the setbacks for his decrees pushed the Peronist government to invite trade unions back for fresh talks with business leaders to try to reform labor laws by consensus.
The three-way talks are due to begin this week.
